text:
A: Hi! Hello, can you hear me okay?
B: Yeah. Hi. Adam.
A: Elira. Sorry, I'm a bit flustered, my last one was really nice actually, we talked about tax codes, which I never thought I'd say.
B: Ha. Right.
A: So what do you do? I feel like I've asked everyone that, sorry.
B: It's fine. I'm a stonemason. Er, repair work on old sandstone buildings round Bradford. Chapels, mills, terraces, a lot of listed stuff.
A: Oh, that's so cool. Like, actual stone, with a chisel?
B: Actual stone, yeah. Half the week I'm in the workshop dressing blocks, half on scaffolding putting them in.
A: Is it not freezing on scaffolding?
B: Er, the workshop's worse, honestly. In January it's a big shed with the doors open for the forklift. You're stood there in two fleeces and you still can't feel your hands. Site's at least got a bit of sun some days.
A: Oh God. I'd be useless. I complain if the 34 bus is ten minutes late and I'm standing at the stop.
B: Ha. Where are you, London?
A: Walthamstow, yeah. I'm between jobs at the minute, I was an office coordinator for a property management company. So, erm, I've probably sent stonemasons emails, to be honest, chasing quotes.
B: Probably. We get a lot of them. Usually somebody wanting it done by Friday.
A: Sorry! That was literally my job, though. Somebody upstairs would go "why isn't it done" and I'd be the one ringing you. Ringing someone like you, I mean.
B: It's alright. Somebody's got to do it. Most of the time it's the stone that's slow, not us.
A: What do you mean, the stone's slow?
B: Er, so if it's a listed building you can't just use any sandstone, it's got to match, colour and grain and how it weathers. So you're waiting on a quarry to find the right bed. Then you've got to make templates off the old bit, cut it, dress it. One window head might be a week's work on its own. People see it and think it's just a block.
A: Okay, I'm never chasing anyone again. Do you like it, though?
B: Yeah. I do. I'd like more carving, that's the bit I'm after. Maybe cathedral work one day.
A: That's lovely. What do you do when you're not freezing in a shed?
B: Walking, mostly. Up on Ilkley Moor, Baildon. I'll go out on a Sunday and be back for tea.
A: Tea, see, everyone up north says tea. I'd say dinner.
B: Tea's at six. Dinner's at dinnertime.
A: Ha, no, that's lunch! Erm, I walk a lot too, round the Wetlands, it's flat though. No moors in Walthamstow.
B: Flat's fine. My knees'd like flat.
A: Do you live up there with family or?
B: With my mum and dad, at the minute. Saving for a house.
A: Honestly, that's so sensible. My mum would've loved it if I'd stayed at home. I moved in with my boyfriend and she didn't speak to me properly for about two months.
B: Oh, right.
A: It's fine now, she feeds him more than she feeds me. Sorry, that was a lot of information.
B: No, it's fine. My mum's a bit like that with my sister's kids. Er, did you do the puzzle at the start? I've been asking everyone, I was rubbish.
A: Oh, I panicked. I kept going back and changing them. Does that make sense? Like I'd get it right and then
